body.text: In short:
The new treaty will require Solomon Islands to consult with Australia on national security and sensitive infrastructure.
Yesterday it was revealed Solomon Islands would not renew its security deal with China.
What's next?
Under the new deal, Australia will help strengthen Solomon Islands's police force and create opportunities for its citizens to work in aged care and childcare in Australia.

Solomon Islands has vowed to ensure its critical infrastructure is free from "militarisation and unauthorised access" and that it will never allow a foreign military base on its soil in a landmark new agreement with Australia.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale both hailed the "historic" treaty after a signing ceremony in Canberra, watched on by a large contingent of Solomon Islands ministers and MPs.
But Mr Wale declined to confirm that his government would scrap its 2022 security pact with China, saying he was unable to discuss the deal.
The ABC confirmed yesterday that Mr Wale's government had quietly informed China that it would let the contentious security agreement phase out when it came up for renewal in April next year.
Mr Wale told journalists in Parliament House that "unfortunately, there is a non-disclosure clause in the treaty with China, the security pact and the policing agreement".
"So I am unable to talk about that. We have ongoing discussions with China,"
he said.
"But of course, today is about our relationship with Australia and the treaty that we've signed today."
Mr Albanese described the treaty as a "new chapter in our partnership to strengthen our shared prosperity and our security".

He said Australia would open up new migration pathways for Solomon Islanders who wanted to work in Australia in aged care and child care, as well as liberalise visa arrangements for its citizens and plough more money into key development priorities for Solomon Islands — including Mr Wale's signature free education policy.

Under the treaty, Solomon Islands has committed that "its sensitive infrastructure shall remain free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access" and that it will not "permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base".

While it does not explicitly ban security partnerships with outside players such as China, the treaty says Solomon Islands will "ensure security cooperation comes from Pacific Islands Forum [PIF] members" and safeguard regional security if it forms any partnerships for "security needs unable to be met by PIF members".

Mr Wale said that under his nation's previous government, Solomon Islands had been "a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region" — in a thinly-veiled reference to the Sogavare government's security pact with China.
"Those days are done, gone," he said.

"The treaty not only resets our relationship with Australia, but it elevates it to an enduring one, one that there is trust and certainty and one that puts us, Solomon Islands, in the position of being a trusted, reliable partner in the region."

Mr Albanese said the treaty cemented Australia's view that "the priority for security cooperation comes from PIF members and it states very clearly that Australia remains the Solomon Islands' security partner of choice".
Major diplomatic victory
The government has been careful not to skite about the deal, but still sees the treaty — along with Mr Wale's commitment to let the China security agreement phase out — as a major diplomatic win.
Former Australian high commissioner to Solomon Islands Lachlan Strahan called the treaty a "major step forward" and said the labour mobility and education provisions were "very significant".
"Locking in Australia's standing as the primary security partner of Solomon Islands in a legally binding document is also very significant," he said.
"Remember that the security agreement between China and Solomon Islands was not legally binding … Now it has been relegated to the past, at least for the time being."
Dr Strahan said the provisions banning foreign military or security bases and keeping critical infrastructure free from militarisation were also important.
"[Former prime minister Manasseh] Sogavare was true to his word not to allow a Chinese base in the country," he said.
"But it is much better to have a formal legal commitment to such a bar."
Mr Wale's pivot away from China and towards Australia is likely to generate political controversy in Solomon Islands.

Mr Sogavare, who is now the opposition leader, warned on Monday that scrapping the China policing pact could undermine development ties with Beijing, and he suggested Mr Wale was dancing to Australia's tune.
Mr Wale stared down an aborted motion of no confidence earlier this year, and told reporters in Canberra he was confident in his position.
"The decision to sign this treaty is a decision taken by my caucus and my entire cabinet. There was unanimity to sign and so that's what we've done," he said.
"I welcome another motion of no confidence. I look forward to it."
Anthony Albanese said the strong showing of Solomon Islands MPs and ministers in Canberra "signifies the strength of support from both sides for this agreement".
Dr Strahan said Mr Wale's numbers were strong right now because he "recently peeled away several members of the opposition to join his ranks".
"But Solomons' politics is inherently volatile," he said.
"Without strong party structures and platforms and a high number of independents, political configurations shift often sometimes quite suddenly."
